args.text: Decoy test on Core Tee. The case for cutting: incremental CM if removed is -$5.1k, so cutting gains +$5.1k, but only if zero baskets are lost. The case for keeping: the tee is in 47% of mixed multi-item baskets (4,386 orders, avg $73.85 CM each, about $324k of CM). The loss is concentrated in tee-only orders: 3,527 orders at -$4.58 avg, and TEE2FOR50 pairs at exactly $50 ship free, at -15% CM. So the tee's 'loss' is really the free-shipping threshold acting on tee pairs. Allocation also matters: -$5.3k by revenue, -$20.5k by units. Mixed baskets with the tee are not more profitable per order than those without ($74 vs $84), so the halo is unproven. I'll quantify the breakeven halo instead of assuming it.

args.text: Threshold choice. At 12% abandon, $100 looks best (+$41.5k), but it starts charging the single full-price core item ($78 polo, $88 linen, $98 chino), which is where conversion risk is highest. Stress test: $75 stays positive even at 40% abandon (+$12.4k). $100 flips to -$20.3k at 40%. Pick $75. It sits just below the cheapest full-price core item, so it catches tee pairs and discounted singles and leaves the core customer alone. At $75 the $50-60 band is no longer CM-negative. The conversion trade-off is an explicit assumption: 12% abandon, no trade-up upside. Propose an A/B test before a full rollout.

args.text: WELCOME30 counter-check. The cohort is weaker but not worthless: $42 tenure-matched CM per customer vs $81 for full-price acquired, and an $18 first order vs $49. They repeat just as often (45% vs 42%), but 66% of their repeat orders use a promo code, vs 4% for full-price acquired. Only 10% convert to full price (253 customers, $81 CM each, about the same as a typical full-price customer). Customers acquired with other promo codes behave like full-price ones (40% FP conversion), so this is a WELCOME30 problem, not a promo problem. Killing the code risks losing positive-CM customers. Marketing spend/CAC isn't in the mirror, so payback can't be checked; that's a data gap. Model the options instead of killing it.

Data gaps: no marketing spend/CAC, no air-freight rates, no exchange data.
